p098.lead: Through Greek philosophy, the Roman state religion, the mystery cults, and Mithraism to Christianity: the long westward journey of the Salem teachings.

p098.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p098.s0.h: Introduction — Echoes of Salem in the West
p098.s0.b0: Following the Hebrew prophets of the previous paper, Paper 98 traces the path the Melchizedek teachings took in Europe and the Western world. They came chiefly by way of Egypt, were thoroughly Hellenized and later Christianized, and settled into Occidental philosophy. The Salem missionaries were gradually absorbed into many cults, but the group that kept their teachings in the purest form was the Cynics.
p098.s0.b1: The teachings did not travel by one road only. The paper adds that much of the Salem doctrine was spread in Europe by Jewish mercenary soldiers who fought in many Western wars. Truth moves not only through the preaching of missionaries but through unexpected people and channels.
p098.s0.b3: One question unlocks this paper: what grows from the seed of truth depends on the soil it falls into. In Greece the seed was received as philosophy, in Rome as state ceremony, and among the Mediterranean masses as mystery cult, each in its own shape.
p098.s1.h: I. The Salem Religion among the Greeks — Zeus Bound by Fate
p098.s1.b0: The Salem missionaries kept the oath of ordination imposed by Machiventa: they would organize no exclusive congregations, never function as priests, and receive for their service nothing but food, clothing, and shelter. The author believes that, had they not interpreted this pledge so strictly, they might have built up a great religious structure among the Greeks.
p098.s1.b1: The Hellenic invaders brought anthropomorphic God concepts with them, and Dyaus-Zeus became head of the Greek pantheon. But because the Greeks kept Fate in control above the gods, they never reached a true monotheism. The intelligent Greeks neither greatly loved nor greatly feared the Olympian gods, and thanks to the antipriestcraft influence of the Salem teachers, no priesthood of any importance ever arose in Greece.
p098.s1.b3: Greek mythology was more aesthetic than ethical. It helped in picturing a universe governed by a group of deities, but Greek morals, ethics, and philosophy soon far outran the god concept. The author warns that this imbalance between intellectual and spiritual growth proved as hazardous to Greece as it had been in India.
p098.s2.h: II. Greek Philosophic Thought — When Believing Bows to Thinking
p098.s2.b0: The Olympian religion, which promised no salvation, had nearly vanished within a thousand years. When the Orient and the Levant experienced a new awakening to monotheism in the sixth century before Christ, the Greeks looked instead for comfort in philosophy and metaphysics. They succeeded in mastering fear, but they did not see that true religion is the cure for soul hunger and moral despair.

head: Thinker
What the paper reports
rows: Elevated the ideals of religion but developed no technique for conserving the highest values
Taught one God, but a deity too pantheistic to be a personal Father
A mechanist, except that he recognized a First Cause, an Initial Mind
Virtue is knowledge; goodness is health of the soul; it is wrong to return evil for evil; wisdom, courage, temperance, justice

p098.s2.b3: The author sets Greece and Palestine side by side to show how the church as an institution shapes culture. In one, priests and scripture controlled thought until dogma hardened; in the other, the absence of priests and sacred scriptures left thought free, yet religion as personal experience lagged behind.

head: Greece
Palestine
rows: A startling development in depth of thought
The preservation of morality and religion
God dissolving into a misty vapor of pantheistic speculation
Dogma so crystallized as to jeopardize growth

p098.s2.b5: Ordinary people wanted not abstract philosophy but promises of salvation and a personal God who could hear their prayers. That longing poured into the mystery cults—the Eleusinian mysteries, Dionysus worship, the Orphic brotherhood—and the author records how quickly and deeply Greece fell from its heights of philosophy. The conclusion is that philosophy, religion, and science must be welded into one.
p098.s3.h: III. The Melchizedek Teachings in Rome — Religion in Service of the State
p098.s3.b0: Latin religion had a strongly political character from the start. Too few Salem missionaries reached Italy, and the gods and temples of the Etruscan priesthood were organized into the Roman state religion. Rome took in the Greek gods wholesale—Zeus became Jupiter, Aphrodite became Venus—and the religious initiation of Roman youths was their solemn consecration to the service of the state.
p098.s3.b1: Rome conquered politically but was conquered in turn by the cults of Egypt, Greece, and the Levant. Augustus tried to revive the old state religion, and after hearing of the earlier Salem attempts to teach one God, he ended by proclaiming himself the supreme god. The Cynics, who made the last stand for the Salem faith, were rejected by the people at large.
p098.s3.b2: The worship of Augustus flourished across the empire during his lifetime, except in Palestine. This era of human gods went on until the official cult counted more than two-score self-elevated human deities, all claiming miraculous births and superhuman attributes. Once the idea of one God fell into the hands of power, it was turned to the exaltation of men as gods.
p098.s4.h: IV–V. The Mystery Cults; The Cult of Mithras — A Hunger for Salvation
p098.s4.b0: Having lost their family and state religions and being unable to grasp philosophy, the masses of the Greco-Roman world turned to mystery cults that promised comfort now and immortality after death. The paper names the three most popular.

head: Cult
Central deity
What the paper describes
rows: Commemorated death and resurrection; the “day of blood”; impressive but degrading
A resurrection legend drawn from the revival of vegetation; more refined
A savior and redeemer of a sinful race; eventually displaced the other two

p098.s4.b3: Mithraism spread across the empire with Roman legions recruited in the Levant. By the time it reached Rome it had absorbed many of Zoroaster’s teachings and was much improved, and it was chiefly through this cult that Zoroaster’s religion later influenced Christianity. Its followers worshiped in caves, believed that partaking of the sacrament ensured eternal life, and held their most elaborate festival on December twenty-fifth.
p098.s4.b4: The Mithraic story included water gushing from a rock, a flood, a last supper before the god ascended into the heavens, and a final judgment. At first only men could be initiated, through seven successive orders; women were later admitted to the adjoining temples of the Great Mother. This fact connects with the point that decided the contest between the two religions in the next section.
p098.s5.h: VI. Mithraism and Christianity — What Decided the Contest
p098.s5.b0: During the third century after Christ the two religions looked very much alike. Most places of worship were underground, and both practiced baptism and partook of the sacrament of bread and wine. Yet Mithraism encouraged militarism while Christianity was ultrapacific. The deciding factor lay elsewhere.
p098.s5.b2: Here the author adds a balanced observation about institutions. The religions of Greece and Rome lacked any powerful agency for preserving higher values. It is true that institutionalization tends to lower the spiritual quality of religion, but no religion has yet survived without some degree of institutional organization.
p098.s6.h: VII. The Christian Religion — A Faith Woven from Seven Strands
p098.s6.b0: The final section begins by setting the purpose of the bestowal straight. A Creator Son did not take on mortal flesh to reconcile an angry God, but to win all mankind to the recognition of the Father’s love and the realization of their sonship with God. The paper then explains that Christianity took shape as a compound of many elements.

head: Element of Christianity
What it contributed
rows: A basic factor in all the religions of East and West for four thousand years
Morality, ethics, theology, belief in Providence and the supreme Yahweh

The human life of Joshua ben Joseph and the glorified Christ
Well-intentioned letters later regarded as the “word of God”
Joined with Paul’s theology, still the basis of European ethics

p098.s6.b2: Notice the place of Greek philosophy in this list. The paper holds that Greek thought harmonized with Paul’s version of Christianity better than with any other religious system of the time, and that this was an important factor in Christianity’s success in the West. The missionary zeal of Jesus’ followers equaled that of the Sethites and Salemites and of their Buddhist contemporaries.
p098.s6.b3: The author says that well-meaning teachers like Paul must not be held accountable for the use later generations made of their writings. Even so, he observes that as Christianity became Occidentalized it began to lose its potential appeal to all races and kinds of men.
p098.s7.b0: Paper 98 closes nearly four thousand years of the story of Machiventa’s teachings and judges that he achieved the purpose of his bestowal. When Michael came, the God concept already lived in human hearts, and it still flames anew in living spiritual experience today. The lesson the paper leaves is balance: thought without faith, or faith whose thinking has hardened, will both lose the way.

p098.s7.b2: The next paper, Paper 99, “The Social Problems of Religion,” asks what part such institutional religion ought to play amid the changes of modern society.
p099.lead: Religion’s place in a time of rapid change: not to redesign the social order directly, but to stabilize the ideals of civilization by spiritualizing the individual.

p099.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p099.s0.h: Introduction — Serving Best by Standing Apart
p099.s0.b0: Paper 99 brings the history of religion traced in the two preceding papers to bear on present-day problems. Its author, a Melchizedek of Nebadon, states the principle of the whole paper in its first sentence: religion renders its highest social service when it is least entangled with the secular institutions of society.
p099.s0.b2: In past ages social reform was largely confined to the moral realm, so religion could devote itself to replacing evil with good within the existing order. In the twentieth century, however, religion is called on to adjust to extensive and continuing social reconstruction. True religion opposes violence as a means of social evolution, but it does not oppose society’s intelligent efforts to adapt its institutions to new conditions.
p099.s1.h: I. Religion and Social Reconstruction — A Compass on the High Seas
p099.s1.b0: Mechanical inventions and the spread of knowledge are reshaping civilization, and the coming social order will not settle down for a millennium. Mankind must accept a procession of changes, adjustments, and readjustments on its march toward an unrevealed planetary destiny. Religion has no new duties in such an age, but it is urgently needed as a wise guide and experienced counselor.
p099.s1.b2: Society is becoming more mechanical, more compact, and more interdependent. Religion must act as the **cosmic salt** that keeps these new relationships from becoming mutually destructive. A godless humanitarianism is a noble gesture, the paper says, but true religion is the only power that can lastingly make one group responsive to the sufferings of another.
p099.s2.h: II. Weakness of Institutional Religion — Caught in a Vicious Circle
p099.s2.b0: Institutional religion cannot lead the coming age of reconstruction, because it has become an organic part of the very social order that must be rebuilt. It cannot reconstruct society without first reconstructing itself, and it cannot reconstruct itself until society has been reconstructed. Only the real religion of personal spiritual experience can break out of this deadlock.
p099.s2.b1: For this reason religionists must work in society, industry, and politics **as individuals**, not as groups or parties. The moment a religious group acts collectively in nonreligious affairs, it becomes a political party or an economic organization. Nor are religious people automatically better reformers; they are of more value only insofar as their religion has given them the social wisdom born of the desire to love God and every man as a brother.

head: Institutional religion
The religion of living experience
rows: An organic part of the established order
Traditionalized and dogmatized, slow to adjust
A moral stabilizer and social guide
A glorification of the established order
Wisdom born of knowing God and striving to be like him
The right attitude of the church
Teaching peaceful evolution in place of violent revolution

p099.s3.h: III. Religion and the Religionist — Influence through Individuals
p099.s3.b0: Early Christianity was entirely free from civil entanglements and economic alliances. The kingdom of heaven is neither a social nor an economic order; it is a spiritual brotherhood of God-knowing individuals. Such a brotherhood is nevertheless an amazing social phenomenon in itself, with far-reaching political and economic repercussions.
p099.s3.b1: The religionist is not indifferent to social suffering or injustice. Religion influences civilization directly by spiritualizing the individual citizen, and indirectly as those citizens become influential members of many groups. A high civilization first requires the ideal type of citizen. Many reformers who reject institutional religion are themselves driven by unrecognized religious motives, but since they are not open to religious criticism, they find it hard to correct themselves.
p099.s3.b3: Religion is always in danger of distortion, as when in wartime it is turned into military propaganda, and loveless zeal always harms it. The paper names five ways to keep religion free from unholy secular alliances.

head: What keeps religion free
The danger it guards against
rows: 2. Freedom from social, economic, and political alliances
Becoming a tool of secular power
4. Progressive enhancement of spiritual insight and appreciation of cosmic values
5. The compensations of the scientific mental attitude

p099.s3.b5: In sum, religionists as a group must concern themselves with nothing but religion, yet any one of them, as an individual citizen, may become an outstanding leader of a social, economic, or political reform movement. The business of religion is to create, sustain, and inspire in such citizens a cosmic loyalty that carries them through the hard work of social service.
p099.s4.h: IV. Transition Difficulties — Between the Religion of Fear and the Religion of Love
p099.s4.b0: Genuine religion makes the religionist socially fragrant and lends new meaning to family, school, play, and humor. A living and growing faith, together with children, is the great unifier of family life. But if religion is to build character it must not be standardized; if it is to act as a lure of values it must not be stereotyped; and if it is to inspire supreme loyalties it must not be formalized.
p099.s4.b2: What, then, makes religion genuine? The paper’s test is simple. Whatever upheavals civilization undergoes, a religion is genuine and worth while if it fosters in the individual an experience in which truth, beauty, and goodness are sovereign. Through love and worship this becomes fellowship with man and sonship with God. Religion becoming more and more a private matter is no danger, so long as it does not lose its motivation for unselfish service.
p099.s4.b3: Amid the upheavals of the scientific age, thousands are anxious, restless, and fearful, and they need the consolation of sound religion as never before. The greatest spiritual danger, the author says, is **partial progress**: forsaking the evolutionary religion of fear without yet grasping the revelatory religion of love. Modern science and psychology have weakened only those religions that rest on fear and superstition.

head: Partial approach to reality
Held by
rows: Spiritistic belief in a providential Deity
The way of harmony: a triune existence of spirit, mind, and energy
The revelatory presentation of religion, philosophy, and cosmology

p099.s5.h: V. Social Aspects of Religion — Goals, Not Creeds
p099.s5.b0: Religion is the personal experience of knowing God as a Father, but that experience necessarily leads to knowing man as a brother, and so it acquires a social side. Religion begins as inner adjustment and grows into social service. As long as people like to gather together, religious groups will come into existence.
p099.s5.b2: The paper foresees a day when religionists will cooperate on the basis of unity of ideals and purposes rather than theological opinion. Let “faith” mean the individual’s relation to God, not a creed a group has agreed upon. Jesus did not ask his followers to recite a form of words; he asked them to gather and share the supper of remembrance of his life.
p099.s5.b4: The author also speaks of how to regard other traditions. It is a great mistake, while presenting Christ as the supreme spiritual leader, to require people to reject the God-knowing leaders who brought light to their own peoples in past ages. He adds that the doctrine of the total depravity of man undermined religion’s uplifting power, and that Jesus sought to restore human dignity by declaring all men the children of God.
p099.s5.b5: Primitive man danced out his religion rather than putting it into words; modern man has thought out many creeds and tests of faith. The paper says the religionists of the future must live out their religion and dedicate themselves to the service of the brotherhood of man, with an experience so personal and sublime that it lies too deep for words.
p099.s6.b1: The author does not read the religious turmoil of the twentieth century as spiritual decline. Confusion may come before destruction, but it also comes before growth. His diagnosis—that sectarianism is a disease of institutional religion and dogmatism an enslavement of the spiritual nature—reads as a warning meant to steer that confusion toward growth.
p099.s6.b2: This does not mean the paper rejects religious groups. Group activity dramatizes the loyalties of religion, fosters unselfish fellowship, family life, and religious education, and makes group worship possible. But the more religion is institutionalized, the more its power for good is curtailed and its possibilities for evil multiplied. The paper lists these dangers at length.

What follows

The saving message of the gospel gradually lost

p099.s6.b4: The last section sums up religion’s distinctive contribution. Religion should stand aloof from secular activities yet do nothing to hinder the coordination of social institutions. In all reconstruction it provides a stabilizing loyalty to a transcendent object, a goal beyond the immediate one. Without meditating in the presence of God’s sovereignty, no one can wisely decide temporal issues or rise above self-interest.
p099.s7.b0: The conclusion of Paper 99 is balance. Science sobers the dreamer, economic necessity ties him to reality, and personal religious experience brings him face to face with the eternal realities of cosmic citizenship. Religion’s task is not to design society directly but to build a cosmic loyalty in the people who will lead it.

p099.s7.b2: The next paper, Paper 100, “Religion in Human Experience,” looks more deeply at how the personal religious experience emphasized here grows and bears fruit within a single life.
p100.lead: Religion cannot be learned or borrowed; it must grow. The soil and habits of growth, how to tell true conversion from mysticism, and the path toward the balanced personality of Jesus.

p100.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p100.s0.h: Introduction — From the Ordinary Person to a Personality of Power
p100.s0.b0: Where Paper 99 dealt with religion’s place in society, Paper 100 turns to its starting point, the inner life of a single person. Its author, a Melchizedek of Nebadon, says that dynamic religious living transforms the mediocre individual into a personality of idealistic power. Religion serves the progress of all by fostering the progress of each, and love supplies the soil in which that growth takes place.
p100.s1.h: I. Religious Growth — The Loyal Tadpole
p100.s1.b0: A child judges experience by its pleasure; maturity is measured by how far personal pleasure gives way to higher meanings. Some people are too busy to grow, and the chief hindrances to growth are prejudice and ignorance. A child should be given the chance to grow his own religious experience rather than having a ready-made adult experience forced on him. What children carry with them permanently is not precept or even example, but the loyalty of the adults around them.
p100.s1.b3: This does not mean we should simply sit and wait. The paper names, quite concretely, the soil that growth requires and the habits that favor it. The factors may be intentional, but the growth itself is always unconscious—and “unconscious” here means not the subconscious but creative activity on the superconscious levels of mind.

head: The soil of growth
Habits that favor growth
rows: Curiosity and the enjoyment of reasonable adventure
Recognition of religious living in others
The fear stimulus of attention and awareness
A normal consciousness of smallness, humility
Sharing one’s spiritual life with one’s fellows
Living as in the presence of God

p100.s1.b5: Religious experience is strongly influenced by physical health, inherited temperament, and social environment. Yet none of these can block the inner progress of a soul dedicated to doing the Father’s will. Every normal mortal has an innate drive toward growth, and the sure way to foster it is to maintain an attitude of wholehearted devotion to supreme values.
p100.s2.h: II. Spiritual Growth — The Unassailable Citadel of the Spirit
p100.s2.b0: Spiritual development depends on two things: keeping a living connection with true spiritual forces, and bearing spiritual fruit by passing on to others what we have received. Growth begins with an awakening to needs, moves on to a discernment of meanings, and then to a discovery of values. This whole experience is the reality of religion, as distinct from mere theological belief.
p100.s2.b2: Religion grown in this way works on three levels of personality: upon the mind, in the evolving soul, and with the indwelling spirit. Actual spiritual status is measured by attunement with the Thought Adjuster, and its goal is the maximum of Godlikeness. The paper calls eternal life an endless quest for infinite values.
p100.s2.b3: Mortals are entitled to physical pleasures and human affections, but these are not the eternal foundations on which an immortal personality is built. That is why the God-knowing person is not shaken when worldly securities collapse. Spirit-born individuals can calmly stand by while their fondest hopes crash, knowing such catastrophes to be redirections that prepare for more enduring realities.
p100.s3.h: III. Concepts of Supreme Value — Meaning, Value, and Growth
p100.s3.b0: Religion is not a technique for attaining a static, blissful peace of mind; it is an impulse that organizes the soul for dynamic service. Human likes and dislikes do not determine good and evil. This section draws careful distinctions among the concepts that surround value.

head: Concept
What the paper says
rows: What experience adds to value; the appreciative consciousness of values
Experienced when realities are meaningfully associated and recognized by mind; never static
The experiential realization of value when the actual and the potential are joined
Always meaningful, but relatively valueless without growth
Recognizing the growth of value, the progress of meaning, and their interrelation—God-consciousness

p100.s3.b3: Man cannot cause growth; he can only supply favorable conditions for it. Love grows in just this way. Social growth cannot be secured by legislation, nor moral growth by improved administration. Man’s sole contribution to growth is the mobilization of all the powers of his personality—living faith.
p100.s4.h: IV. Problems of Growth — Through Conflict, by Understanding, to Love
p100.s4.b0: New meanings emerge only amid conflict. There is no growth without psychic conflict and spiritual agitation, and the slothful animal mind rebels at the effort of wrestling with cosmic problems. The great task of religious living is to unify the personality by the dominance of love, and the highest happiness is inseparably linked with spiritual progress.
p100.s4.b1: The most practical passage of this section concerns love. When someone irritates you, the paper advises, try sympathetically to understand his viewpoint and the reasons behind his conduct. The picture of the cave dweller makes the point: a snarling man with a raised club, once you see the saber-toothed tiger before him and the woman and children behind him, becomes the beginning of the nobility of protecting one’s family.
p100.s5.h: V. Conversion and Mysticism — The River Bed Is Not the River
p100.s5.b0: The world is full of souls lost in the sense of direction. The paper says that few have learned to put a philosophy of living in the place of religious authority, yet it adds that the symbols of socialized religion should not be despised, for though the river bed is not the river, it is a channel of growth. Growth leads from stagnation through conflict to coordination, and from the bondage of fear to the liberty of divine sonship.
p100.s5.b1: Conversion may come gradually or suddenly at a moment of crisis. The paper cites both Paul on the Damascus road and Gautama Siddhartha seeking truth alone, and notes that many true believers have progressed without any sudden conversion. Most conversion phenomena are psychological, but when the mobilization of mind and the motivation of loyalty are complete, a truly spiritual experience can occur in which the indwelling spirit grasps the believer’s consecrated purpose.
p100.s5.b3: On mysticism the paper is cautious. Trancelike visionary states should never be cultivated as religious experience, and the very conditions that bring them on—fatigue, fasting, fear, wild dancing—reveal their danger. Much of what emerges from them comes from the subconscious mind. The better way is living faith, sincere worship, and unselfish prayer, and Jesus never resorted to such methods for communion with the Father.
p100.s5.b4: The author also asks for consistency in how we picture the mind. If we accept a subconscious mind as a working hypothesis, we should also posit a corresponding superconscious level, the zone of contact with the Thought Adjuster. The danger in such speculation is that strange dreams and visions may be mistaken for divine communications. In the past, divine beings revealed themselves to God-knowing persons not because of their mystic trances but in spite of them.
p100.s6.h: VI–VII. Marks of Religious Living; The Acme of Religious Living — The Balanced Personality
p100.s6.b0: Religion is not a specific function of life but a mode of living. The outstanding mark of all religion is wholehearted devotion to supreme values, and a religion is genuine to the extent that the value it holds supreme is a real spiritual reality. The truly religious person is not socially isolated, keeps his sense of humor, and knows the peace that passes understanding.
p100.s6.b2: Evolutionary religion, being a genuine experience, also has its loyalty and grandeur. But revelatory religion adds a new quality, divine wisdom, and leads to a deeper consciousness of the Fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. The capacity to receive that wisdom is developed through experience in and with the human religions.
p100.s6.b3: The final section finds the acme of religious living in the personality of Jesus. The average person cannot hope to reach his perfection, but anyone can develop a strong and unified personality along his lines. What was unique in the Master’s personality was not so much its perfection as its **symmetry**, its exquisitely balanced unification.
p100.s6.b5: He was not a man of sorrows but a soul of gladness, often saying “⟦Q 100:7.9⟧Be of good cheer.⟦/Q⟧” He was indignant at sin but never angry at the sinner, never in a hurry, and respectful even of the faulty worship of his fellows. The most original of his teachings was the emphasis on love and mercy in place of fear and sacrifice.
p100.s6.b6: Jesus lived the truth as he taught it, free of hypocrisy and affectation. His heart embraced all mankind, and his invitation was always “⟦Q 100:7.6⟧Whosoever will, let him come.⟦/Q⟧” As a man among men he trusted the Father as a little child trusts his parent, and apparent failure never shook him.
p100.s7.b0: Paper 100 pictures religion not as a possession but as a growing life. We cannot cause the growth ourselves, but we can tend its soil, cultivate its habits, and refuse to run from its conflicts. At the end of that road stands the example of Jesus, who still unifies life, ennobles character, and simplifies experience today.

p100.s7.b2: The next paper, Paper 101, “The Real Nature of Religion,” examines more philosophically what the religious experience described here rests on: revelation, faith, and the work of the Adjuster.
p101.lead: Religion is faith, trust, and assurance: religion as spiritual insight shared with the Adjuster, the role and limits of revelation, and the liberation that faith brings.

p101.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p101.s0.h: Introduction — Religion Is More Than a Moral Movement
p101.s0.b0: Paper 101 is the most philosophical of the Melchizedek series on religion. Religion ranges from the primitive fear slavery of the savage to the faith liberty of those who are conscious of sonship with God. It is the ancestor of advanced ethics and morals, yet in itself it is not merely a moral movement.
p101.s0.b1: From the outset the author says that religious assurance is more than an emotional feeling; it transcends the reason of the mind and even the logic of philosophy. It is this assurance that triumphs over the logic of despair born in the unbelieving material mind.
p101.s1.h: I. True Religion — Through Thought, Not Feeling
p101.s1.b0: True religion is neither a philosophic system proved by natural evidence nor an ecstasy enjoyed only by mystics. It is not the product of reason, yet seen from within it is altogether reasonable; it is not derived from philosophy, yet as experience it is altogether logical. The Thought Adjuster has no special mechanism for self-expression, so religious experience takes place through the natural mechanism of the mortal mind.
p101.s1.b2: The divine spirit contacts us not through emotions but in the realm of the highest and most spiritualized thinking. Religion, then, is not the search for new facts or unusual experiences, but the discovery of new spiritual meanings in facts already known. When the sense of evolutionary duty and the illumination of revelation make a deep enough impression, a person finally concludes that he has no right not to believe in God.
p101.s2.h: II. The Fact of Religion — The First Cause of Science and the God of Salvation
p101.s2.b0: The fact of religion lies wholly in the religious experience of rational and average human beings. The proof that revelation is revelation lies in the same experience: revelation unites the apparently divergent sciences of nature and the theology of religion into one consistent universe philosophy.

head: Science
Religion
Philosophy
Revelation

The hypothesis of a First Cause
Assurance of a God of salvation
Affirms that the First Cause and the God of salvation are one Deity

p101.s2.b2: Nature reveals only a God of motion and offers no logical ground for believing in personal survival. Neither does it rule out seeing the universe as the handiwork of the God of religion. The order matters: the one who first finds God in his own soul then sees the same God in nature.
p101.s2.b4: The realization of religion has never depended on great learning or clever logic. This is why some of the greatest religious teachers had little worldly wisdom, and why faith is open alike to the learned and the unlearned. Among those with a similar experience no argument about God is needed, and to those not sure of God no argument will ever truly convince.
p101.s3.h: III. The Characteristics of Religion — Twelve Marks of Spiritual Faith
p101.s3.b0: Religion is so vital that it survives without learning and even through contamination by mistaken cosmologies and philosophies. Within each person are three spirit endowments that constitute him a spirit personality in potential destiny.

head: Endowment
Its source
rows: The cosmic mind together with the Thought Adjuster, the Father’s gift
The Holy Spirit, the Creative Spirit’s gift
Spiritual philosophy, the wisdom of spirit realities
The Spirit of Truth, the gift of the bestowal Sons

p101.s3.b2: Genuine spiritual faith shows itself in a characteristic way of reacting to trying situations. The paper lists twelve such marks; a few are gathered below. These “unnatural” reactions are named as one of three evidences that a divine spirit dwells within man.

head: Even in the face of
Genuine faith shows
rows: A sublime trust in the goodness of God
The perplexing presence of evil and sin
Belief in universe unity and divine guidance

p101.s4.h: IV. The Limitations of Revelation — The Cosmology Is Not Inspired
p101.s4.b0: This section is remarkable because here revelation states its own limits. The revelators may not impart knowledge that humanity has not yet earned or that would be premature. So they say in advance that while the historic facts and religious truths of these papers will stand, many of their statements about the physical sciences will need revision within a few years.
p101.s4.b2: The point of the warning is clear: do not throw away the religious truth because of surface errors in the cosmology. In the end religion is judged by its fruits. Even so, revealed cosmology has great value: it reduces confusion by authoritatively eliminating error, coordinates known facts, restores lost knowledge, fills in gaps, and illuminates the spiritual teachings.
p101.s5.h: V. Religion Expanded by Revelation — From Faith to Truth to Insight
p101.s5.b0: Revelation saves ages upon ages of time that would otherwise be spent sifting the errors of evolution. Science deals with facts, religion with values, and philosophy seeks to unite the meanings of both. Feeling and emotion always accompany religion, but they are not religion.

head: Evolutionary religion
Revealed religion
The morontia stage
rows: Mind; the endowment of the adjutant of worship
Spirit; the bestowal spirits representing the Trinity
Faith plus the living truth of revealed reality
The assurance of truth increasingly replaces that of faith

p101.s5.b2: In the spirit world the assurances of pure spirit insight will operate in place of faith and truth, or rather superimposed upon them. The paper sees this growth already beginning on earth. Where human faith and divine truth work together in practice, a character is formed that is well on the road to a morontia personality.
p101.s6.h: VI. Progressive Religious Experience — The Faith of Jesus and a Sevenfold Salvation
p101.s6.b0: At every stage of religious experience the Thought Adjuster is the secret of the personal realization of the Supreme. Animals have knowledge, but only man has the capacity for wisdom, and truth becomes accessible to the wisdom-endowed mind through the Adjuster and the Spirit of Truth. Michael himself lived under evolutionary religion until his baptism, and from his baptism to the cross under the combined guidance of evolutionary and revealed religion.
p101.s6.b1: The paper says that the teachings of Jesus were the first Urantian religion to harmonize knowledge, wisdom, faith, truth, and love so fully as to give at once tranquillity, certainty, and the assurance of survival. The salvation to which his faith points is sevenfold.

head: Salvation from
How
rows: Realizing sonship with God, who is spirit
Knowing the truth and being made free by it
Realizing the brotherhood of beings and discovering spiritual reality through service
Attaining the harmony of Havona and the perfection of Paradise
Being coordinated with the achievements of other self-conscious beings
An endless life of unending progression
Perfected oneness with Deity in and through the Supreme

p101.s7.h: VII–VIII. A Personal Philosophy of Religion; Faith and Belief
p101.s7.b0: A personal philosophy of religion draws its material from inner and outer experience: social status, education, temperament, vocation, marriage, and more. The paper describes four phases in its evolution. Moral cowards never reach high planes of philosophic thinking; it takes courage to explore unknown realms of thought.

head: Phase
What it looks like
rows: Conforms to tradition and authority; may remain mere submission
Satisfied with just enough to steady daily life; arrested early, letting well enough alone
Advances to logical intellectuality but stagnates in cultural bondage
Free of conventional handicaps; dares to think, act, and live honestly and fearlessly

p101.s7.b2: Accepting a teaching as true is only belief. Belief becomes faith when it motivates life and shapes the way one lives. Beliefs can be held by groups, but faith rises only in the heart of the individual. Living faith does not betray intellectual integrity, foster bigotry or persecution, or hold an unreasoning prejudice against scientific discovery.
p101.s8.h: IX–X. Religion and Morality; Religion as Man’s Liberator
p101.s8.b0: No revelation can be authentic if it ignores the ethical duties fostered by evolutionary religion; revelation always enlarges the ethical horizon. The paper also urges us to judge primitive religion according to the enlightenment and conscience of its people, and not to measure another’s religion by our own standards of knowledge. The search for beauty belongs to religion only insofar as it enriches the moral.
p101.s8.b1: The last section pictures religion as a liberator. Neither physical causation nor the continuity of ideas can free man from the suspense of being a transient creature doomed to extinction. There is no scientific or logical proof of God, but whoever wills to do the will of God comes to comprehend the validity of spiritual values. The person freed by faith is no longer a slave of a mathematical cosmos but a liberated son of the Universal Father, at home in his universe.
p101.s9.b0: Paper 101 locates religion not in argument or emotion but in experience within our highest thinking, shared with the Adjuster. Even revelation admits its limits here and asks to be judged by its fruits. What the paper offers the reader is a balance of assurance and humility: spiritual certainty that does not waver, and knowledge that must always keep growing.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Approach God through your highest thinking rather than through swings of feeling
Do not fear new scientific discoveries
The cosmology is not inspired; human wisdom must evolve
Let accepted beliefs grow into a faith that moves your life
Do not judge another’s religion by your own standards
Judge by their enlightenment and status of conscience
Keep poise and trust in times of trial
The twelve marks of genuine faith

p101.s9.b2: The next paper, Paper 102, “The Foundations of Religious Faith,” builds on the relation between faith and revelation set out here and looks more deeply at where religious assurance is rooted.
p102.lead: One brave stretch of faith dispels the despair of materialism: how faith differs from knowledge, and why it arrives at certainty within experience.

p102.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p102.s0.h: Introduction — The Materialist’s Night and One Step of Faith
p102.s0.b0: Paper 102 opens with a dark picture. To the unbelieving materialist, man is an evolutionary accident, his hope of survival a figment of imagination, and even the devoted labors of the best of men are doomed to vanish into the night of oblivion. The author, a Melchizedek of Nebadon, calls this vision the cry of despair of a soul lost in spiritual darkness.
p102.s0.b2: When is this saving faith born? When man’s moral consciousness realizes that human values can be translated from the material to the spiritual, from the human to the divine, from time to eternity. The whole paper examines, step by step, what this faith rests on and why it does not waver.
p102.s1.h: I. Assurances of Faith — Loving in Order to Know
p102.s1.b0: The Thought Adjuster transforms man’s primitive sense of duty into a higher faith in the realities of revelation. The starting point is a hunger for perfection, and whoever chooses to do the divine will shall know the way of truth. Here the usual order of knowing is reversed.
p102.s1.b2: This does not make doubt a sin. Honest doubts and sincere questions merely mean delay on the journey. Childlike trust gains entrance to the kingdom of ascent, but progress depends on the robust faith of the full-grown person. The certainties of science come from the intellect; the certitudes of religion spring from the foundations of the whole personality.
p102.s1.b4: The paper admits that on Urantia the revelation of truth has often been mixed with transient cosmologies. Teachings about the physical world change year by year, but eternal truth should not be slighted because it is found in company with outdated ideas. God is not proved by miracles or material evidence; we know him because we trust him.
p102.s2.h: II. Religion and Reality — A Religion That Lives and Acts
p102.s2.b0: Religion needs no definition; we recognize it in the lives of others. Believers live as if immortality were already within their grasp, showing a stability and tranquillity that physiology and sociology cannot explain. Genuine assurance is firm, yet it never conveys the slightest impression of self-assertion.
p102.s2.b1: Knowledge is an eternal quest that yields only an increasing probability of approximation, but the spiritually illuminated soul knows, and knows now. Even so, such a person does not lose interest in the progress of science. Philosophy must be founded on material facts, but the soul of its dynamics is spiritual insight.
p102.s2.b2: Even scientific discoveries do not become real in experience until the mind unravels and correlates them into meaning. Mind is unity, and so man seeks to identify the energy unity of his science with the spirit unity of his religion. But this unification is possible only when the mind is firmly aware of material things, intellectual meanings, and spiritual values alike; only in that harmony does personality find the satisfaction of cosmic consistency.
p102.s2.b3: The paper warns against two kinds of people who use religion as a refuge. The indolent hide in stereotyped doctrines and dogmas; the timid use sentimental religion to escape the demands of living. Yet the mission of religion is to prepare man to face the changes of life bravely, even heroically.
p102.s3.h: III. Knowledge, Wisdom, and Insight — Four Kinds of Consciousness
p102.s3.b0: Educational poverty handicaps higher religious attainment, but overdevelopment of the intellectual factors can also hinder it. Religious speculation is inevitable, yet it always falsifies its object. Religion will therefore always be marked by paradox, because we lack the morontia mota that would connect the material and spiritual levels. This section sets science, philosophy, religion, and revelation side by side.

head: Science (knowledge)
Philosophy (wisdom)
Religion (experience)
Revelation
rows: Deals justly with those who differ
Moves us to love and serve others as ourselves
Liberates them for the eternal adventure
Eternal brotherhood: the Corps of the Finality
That the three are one, and good

p102.s3.b2: Religious desire is the hungry search for divine reality; religious experience is the consciousness of having found God. The joy of that discovery overflows not in boasting but in loving service to one’s fellows. Real religion leads to increased social service.
p102.s4.h: IV–V. The Fact of Experience; The Supremacy of Purposive Potential
p102.s4.b0: Because the Adjuster is present in our minds, knowing the mind of God is no more mysterious than knowing any other mind. Experience is the interplay of a questioning self with an external reality, and faith translates our natural awareness of other minds into religion. If God were not a personality, he could not become a living part of such experience.
p102.s4.b1: The error in religious experience is directly proportional to the materialism mixed into it. The paper also observes that modern religions have overemphasized prayer and neglected the more essential communion of worship.
p102.s4.b3: Revealed religion is the unifying element of human existence. Revelation unifies history and coordinates the sciences from geology and astronomy to sociology and psychology. Spiritual experience is the real soul of man’s cosmos.
p102.s4.b4: In the time universes the potential is always supreme over the actual. The transformation of primitive man’s craven fear into living faith is evidence of it. The same principle appears in the relation between morality and religion.

head: Morality
Religion
rows: Discloses an almighty Controller, a Deity to be served
Discloses an all-loving Father, a God to be worshiped and loved

p102.s5.h: VI. The Certainty of Religious Faith — From Probability to Certainty
p102.s5.b0: The advance of science destroys false gods and may cloud spiritual vision for a time, but in the end it clears away the superstition that hid the living God. To isolate one part of life and call it religion distorts both life and religion; this is why the God of worship claims all allegiance or none. The God in whom the mature religionist has faith is not a hypothesis or an idealization but a God of love.

head: To
God is
rows: A certainty, an actuality of religious experience

p102.s5.b2: Faith transforms the God of philosophic probability into the saving God of certainty in personal experience. When a doubter objects that this certainty is not supported by logic, the believer need only ask in return: how do you know that I do not know?
p102.s5.b5: Reason can always question faith, but faith can always supplement reason. God is the first truth and the last fact; as truth he can be known, but to explain him one must explore the universe of universes. Only living faith can bridge the gulf between the experience of the truth of God and our ignorance of the fact of God.
p102.s5.b6: The evidence of this certainty is not argument but the social fruits of the spirit that believers bear. Organic evolution is a fact; purposive evolution is the truth that makes that fact consistent. Materialism, which keeps referring the higher back to the lower, has gone bankrupt, and it cheapens human life.
p102.s6.h: VII. The Certitude of the Divine — No Effects without Causes
p102.s6.b0: The universe is everywhere changing, and a changing universe is a dependent one. The universe and God are not identical: one is effect, and the other is the one self-caused fact. The fact of God is changeless, but the truth of God—his relation to the universe—is ever adapting to the evolving universe.
p102.s6.b2: A person can deny God and still be morally good, loyal, and honest. But the humanistic branches grafted onto such a life bear only social fruits, not spiritual ones, and have no survival value. It takes no great intellect to pick flaws and raise objections; it takes brilliance to answer them, and faith certainty is the greatest technique for dealing with such superficial contentions.
p102.s6.b3: If science or philosophy becomes dogmatic in challenging faith, the God-knowing person may answer with the more farseeing dogmatism of the certainty of experience. The charge of being “unproved” applies equally to the facts of science and the beliefs of philosophy, for they too are experiences in someone’s consciousness. In the end only an absolute can consistently be dogmatic.
p102.s7.h: VIII. The Evidences of Religion — The Experience of Entrusting
p102.s7.b0: The highest evidence of religion lies in experience itself: that man, naturally fearful and suspicious, is willing to entrust his deepest interests to the power and person he calls God. A religion’s standing is best judged by its moral judgments and ethical standards rather than by its civilization, and many of the greatest religious teachers were virtually unlettered.
p102.s7.b1: Personal religion runs ahead of moral evolution, but institutional religion has always lagged behind. Nor is religion ever enhanced by appeals to the miraculous. The highest religion is one person’s experience of seeking God and finding him—the earth life of Jesus of Nazareth.
p102.s8.b0: Paper 102 presents faith not as guesswork filling a gap in knowledge but as the whole personality’s encounter with reality. Its assurance shows itself not in winning arguments but in the fruits of love and service. Because God is the most loving of all friends, we have the right to be most certain of him.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Come to know God by approaching him first in love
Divine things must be loved in order to be known
Do not fear honest doubt, but keep growing in faith
Doubt is not sin, only delay
Do not hide in doctrine; act in daily life
Religion is dynamic and must act
Make time for worship as well as prayer
Bear witness through the fruits of love rather than argument
The social fruits of the spirit are the evidence of certainty

p102.s8.b2: The next paper, Paper 103, “The Reality of Religious Experience,” looks more concretely at how the experience described here grows and shows itself in the individual and in society.
p103.lead: Where religious experience begins and how it grows: from a child’s first unselfish choice to the place where science, philosophy, and revelation meet.

p103.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p103.s0.b0: Where Paper 102 dealt with the foundations of faith, Paper 103 enters the place where that faith is actually experienced. The author, a Melchizedek of Nebadon, begins by naming in turn the influences that sponsor man’s religious responses: the adjutants of worship and wisdom, the Holy Spirit of the Creative Spirit, the Spirit of Truth that follows the bestowal Sons, and the Thought Adjuster.
p103.s0.b2: Religious tendencies are innate in mankind, and primitive religions are always evolutionary in origin. Periodic revelations of truth punctuate their slow progress. As a result, four kinds of religion exist side by side on Urantia today.

head: Kind
Character
rows: Grows from man’s innate religious tendencies
Truth revealed into the course of evolution
A blend of the two in varying degrees
Theologic doctrines built by reasoning and philosophic thought

p103.s1.h: I. Philosophy of Religion — Spiritual Unity, Philosophic Diversity
p103.s1.b0: Religious experience has a unity because the same God fragment indwells each person. But since every personality is unique, no two people interpret its leadings alike. That is why twentieth-century theologians and philosophers produced more than five hundred definitions of religion.
p103.s1.b2: So it matters to know the varied religious experiences of others; otherwise one’s own religion hardens into something egocentric and unsocial. And contrary to the assumption of rationalism, religion begins not with belief but with the pursuit of values. This is why people agree far more easily on goals than on creeds, and why experience persists even when beliefs change greatly.
p103.s1.b4: The experience of realizing spiritual values cannot be named exactly in any human language, and the paper chooses to call it **God-consciousness**. The Adjuster is prepersonal, yet it exudes a flavor of divinity that is personal in the highest sense.
p103.s2.h: II. Religion and the Individual — A Child’s First Unselfish Choice
p103.s2.b0: Religion functions in the mind before it appears in consciousness. Just as a baby is born after nine months, spiritual birth is gradual, yet sooner or later it has its “birth day.” Some pass through anguish like a stormy labor; others grow naturally. Those raised by their parents to know themselves as children of a loving heavenly Father should not look askance at those who reached that awareness only through crisis.
p103.s2.b1: The soil in which revealed religion germinates is the moral nature. A child’s first moral promptings concern not guilt but justice, fairness, and kindness—helping others. The psychology of a child is naturally positive; so many people are negative because they were trained to be.
p103.s2.b3: People tend to identify the selfish urge with the self and the altruistic will with an influence from outside—God—and the paper says this judgment is right, for such unselfish desires originate in the leadings of the indwelling Adjuster. Yet when a personality is not unified, altruism can become so overdeveloped that it injures the self, and a misguided conscience can cause endless unhappiness.
p103.s3.h: III–IV. Religion and the Human Race; Spiritual Communion
p103.s3.b0: Belief in spirits, dreams, and superstitions, along with clan solidarity, shaped primitive religion, but the social group is not the source of religious experience. The true religious impulse comes from spirit presences that activate the will to be unselfish. Religion evolves favorably as magic gives way to morals, and it is destined at last to become the service of God and of man.
p103.s3.b1: What sets a religious gathering apart from a social one is the atmosphere of communion. A shared meal was the earliest form of communion, and the Lord’s Supper continues it. Communion gives a refreshing truce in the conflict between the self-seeking ego and the altruistic urge of the indwelling spirit, and it is the prelude to true worship, the practice of the presence of God.
p103.s3.b3: So a sense of guilt arises in the gap between ideal and practice. The way out is to realize that one’s highest moral ideals are not necessarily the will of God, and to stay true to the purpose of becoming more like him. Jesus swept away the ceremonies of sacrifice and atonement and placed the creature-Creator relationship on a child-parent basis. The Father deals with his children not according to their worthiness but according to their motive and intent.
p103.s4.h: V. The Origin of Ideals — Between Self and Neighbor
p103.s4.b0: Unlike the sense of duty born of fear, the ideal of altruism comes from the direct impulse of the indwelling spirit. The circle of “neighbor” widened from those close at hand to clan and nation, and Jesus enlarged it to all humanity, even to our enemies. Yet the self has rights as well as the neighbor, and neither can claim exclusive service.
p103.s4.b1: Happiness comes when the desires of the self and the altruistic urge of the higher self are reconciled by a unified will. This conflict is not fully resolved within one short life, but every good thing done in this life directly enriches the life to come. Taught that altruistic impulses are merely herd instinct, idealism is fatally wounded; knowing that they come from the spirit, it is mightily energized.
p103.s4.b3: Spiritual growth springs from within the soul, not from pressure, and it is greatest where external pressures are least. The church, then, should let its members interpret their own experience freely.
p103.s5.h: VI. Philosophic Co-ordination — The Morontia Gap
p103.s5.b0: Theology is the study of your own religion; the study of another’s religion is psychology. Seen from outside, the universe looks mechanical, energy and matter; seen from within personality, all creation appears spiritual. Materialism and spiritism each see only a universe turned one way, so neither can build a consistent picture of the cosmos.
p103.s5.b1: Science and religion are hard to reconcile because we know nothing of the intervening domain, the morontia world. The local universe has three stages of reality—matter, morontia, and spirit—and each level has its own technique of knowing.

head: Level
Technique
Description
rows: The understanding technique of the sciences
A supermaterial reality sensitivity: knowledge-reason as substance, faith-insight as essence
A well-meant but futile attempt to make up for the absence of mota
Authoritatively clears the confusion of metaphysics in a world without mota

p103.s5.b5: The highest philosophy, therefore, must rest together on the reason of science, the faith of religion, and the truth insight of revelation. Philosophy must not project reality only along the straight line of logic; it must reckon with the curvature of all relations.
p103.s6.h: VII. Science and Religion — Two Paths Resting on Assumptions
p103.s6.b0: Faith is not founded on reason, yet it is reasonable; it is independent of logic, yet encouraged by sound logic. Ascending man reaches inward toward God and at the same time outward toward an understanding of energy, so the progress of science does not end with earthly life. The two are united through the logic of a philosophy strengthened by revelation.
p103.s6.b1: The paper asks both science and religion for more fearless self-criticism; teachers on both sides are often too self-confident and dogmatic. Neither can prove its own starting point.

head: Its three assumptions
Its act of knowing
rows: The reality of matter, motion, and life
Reason: recognizing the conclusions of physical experience
The validity of mind, spirit, and the universe—the Supreme Being
Faith: recognizing the validity of spiritual consciousness

p103.s6.b4: The presence of the Adjuster is real proof of spiritual reality, but it cannot be demonstrated to the outside world—only to the one who experiences that indwelling. Science discovers the material world, religion evaluates it, and philosophy seeks to interpret its meanings.
p103.s7.h: VIII–IX. Philosophy and Religion; The Essence of Religion
p103.s7.b0: Philosophy can only assume the probability of God; certainty is affirmed only by the experience of a spirit-led person. The experience may be wholly valid while talk about God remains divergent. The paper’s illustration makes the point: a man who loves his wife completely may fail a written examination on the psychology of marital love, yet that does not make his love any less real.
p103.s7.b1: If you know and love God by faith, the paper urges, do not let that experience be diminished by the doubts of science, the caviling of logic, or the clever arguments for a religion without God. It is rather the unbeliever’s doubt that should be challenged. The most helpful philosophy avoids both materialism and pantheism and recognizes the reality of personality, permanence in the presence of change.
p103.s7.b3: The paper names original Buddhism as one of the best religions without a God, yet says that religion without faith is a contradiction. It also warns that when theology dominates religion, religion becomes a doctrine instead of a life.

head: Attainment
The world it opens
Its underlying assumption
rows: The world of facts and things
The universe can be comprehended (the adjutant spirit)
The world of truth and relationships
The material can be coordinated with the spiritual (the spirit of wisdom)
The world of divinity and spiritual experience
God can be known and attained (the Thought Adjuster)

p103.s7.b7: When reason recognizes right and wrong, it shows wisdom; when wisdom chooses between truth and error, it shows spirit leading. Mind, soul, and spirit always work together in this way. Faith leads not merely to a mystical feeling but to knowing God, and it must not be overmuch swayed by its emotional consequences.
p103.s8.b0: Paper 103 pictures religious experience not as theology or emotion but as a living reality that begins with the choice to look past self toward others. Interpretations differ, yet the experience can be true, and its convictions are unassailable. A reader of this paper can be generous toward the faith of others while holding his own experience with courage.

head: Practice
The teaching behind it
rows: Make one choice today that rises above selfishness
An unselfish choice is primitive religious experience
Listen to the religious experiences of others
So that your religion does not become egocentric
Stay true to your purpose even when you fall short of your ideals
Seek unity of spirit rather than agreement in doctrine
A religious group’s security lies in spiritual unity
Do not fear science; be willing to criticize yourself
Both science and religion need self-criticism

p103.s8.b2: The next paper, Paper 104, “Growth of the Trinity Concept,” turns to how religious experience has understood the plurality of Deity—the history and meaning of the Trinity concept.
p104.lead: From man’s habit of thinking in threes to the revelation of the Paradise Trinity: a paper that carefully distinguishes trinity, triunity, and triodity.

p104.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p104.s0.h: Introduction — Triads Are Not the Trinity
p104.s0.b0: Paper 104 begins by drawing a boundary: the Trinity concept of revealed religion must not be confused with the triad beliefs of evolutionary religion. People came to think in threes for homely reasons. Fingers have three joints, three legs are the fewest that will steady a stool, and three support points keep up a tent. For a long time primitive man could not even count beyond three.
p104.s0.b1: Human experience is woven in triads: yesterday, today, and tomorrow; sunrise, noon, and sunset; father, mother, and child. So many peoples, from Persia to Scandinavia, had triad gods, yet these were not true trinities. At times evolutionary triads mingled with revealed concepts until the two could hardly be told apart. The author is a Melchizedek of Nebadon.
p104.s1.h: I. Urantian Trinity Concepts — Revealed Again and Again
p104.s1.b0: The paper reports that the Trinity was presented on Urantia several times, only to fade each time. Each revelation was received differently according to the understanding and existing beliefs of its age.

head: Presentation
By whom and how
What became of it
rows: The staff of Prince Caligastia, about half a million years ago
Lost in the unsettled times after the rebellion
Adam and Eve in the first and second gardens
Survived through the Sethites; carried on in India as Agni, the three-headed fire god
Machiventa Melchizedek — the three concentric circles on his breastplate
Only a very few even remotely grasped the union of Father, Son, and Spirit
Taught his apostles about the persons of the Trinity
The apostles took it as figurative and symbolic

p104.s1.b2: Most of Melchizedek’s disciples thought the Trinity consisted of the three Most Highs of Norlatiadek; a few took it to be the System Sovereign, the Constellation Father, and the local universe Creator Deity. The Salem missionaries spread the teaching through Eurasia and northern Africa, but in later ages it became mixed with the evolutionary triads.
p104.s1.b3: Hinduism developed the trinitarian concept as Being, Intelligence, and Joy, and Buddhism as Teacher, Law, and Brotherhood, and later as Supreme Lord, Holy Spirit, and Incarnate Savior. The paper regards these as real trinitarian postulates: the idea of a threefold manifestation of one God.
p104.s1.b5: The Hebrews and the Muslims, by contrast, in their zeal for the one God, found it hard to distinguish between worshiping three gods and worshiping one Deity in triune manifestation. The paper says the trinity idea takes best hold in religions that combine a firm monotheistic tradition with doctrinal elasticity.
p104.s1.b6: The first Christian trinity, proclaimed at Antioch, consisted of God, his Word, and his Wisdom. Paul knew of the Paradise Trinity, but like the other apostles he confused Jesus, the Creator Son, with the Eternal Son. The Christian concept that gained recognition near the close of the first century was made up of the Universal Father, the Creator Son of Nebadon, and the Divine Minister of Salvington.
p104.s2.h: II. Trinity Unity and Deity Plurality
p104.s2.b0: Monotheism grew as a philosophic protest against the inconsistency of polytheism. It passed through the departmentalizing of the gods, through henotheism, which exalted one god above the many, and finally to the exclusion of all but one. But a solitary God without relationships tends, given time, to be reduced in philosophy to an impersonal Absolute. Trinitarianism grew out of the experiential protest against this difficulty.
p104.s2.b2: The Trinity concept helps us grasp love and law together. One who has come to know the Father’s love through faith soon discovers that this faith does not change the laws of the material universe. Widening horizons require him to recognize, alongside the Paradise Father, the reality of Paradise Deity as universal law—the Trinity sovereignty reaching out even to the local universes.
p104.s2.b4: The Trinity is not the sum of the attributes of the three Deities but a supersummative reality that emerges from their union. Justice is an example. Jesus taught that justice is never a personal act; it is always a group function. The Gods themselves do not administer justice as persons; they do so collectively, as the Trinity.
p104.s2.b6: A mind at home with this concept is prepared to accept other threefold relationships. Theology may be satisfied with the Paradise Trinity, but philosophy and cosmology require the recognition of other triune associations in which the Infinite functions in non-Father capacities—force, energy, causation, potentiality, gravity, pattern, and more.
p104.s3.h: III. Trinities and Triunities — Relationships among the Seven Absolutes
p104.s3.b0: Consistency requires us to see, beyond the Trinity of three Deities, relationships among all seven Absolutes. Reason demands the unity of reality, but finite experience requires the postulate of plural Absolutes and their coordination. Without coordinate existences there could be no diversity of relationships, no qualifying or modifying of the absolute.
p104.s3.b1: Mankind is passing through an age of expanding horizons, and its cosmic philosophy must grow as fast. Man believes in the unity of the cosmos yet sees the diversity of existence; he believes in the changelessness of Deity yet lives in a universe of constant growth. The fullness of infinity must be reconciled with the incompleteness of the evolving universes, and segmented and qualified so that the mortal mind can grasp it.

p104.s3.b3: When the three Paradise persons, as persons, join for united function, they form the first triunity. But this is not a trinity, and the paper carefully distinguishes the two.

p104.s3.b5: There is one point of likeness: both eventuate in functions that are something other than the sum of their members’ attributes. And triunities are very real. Through them the Universal Father exercises immediate and personal control over the master functions of infinity.
p104.s4.h: IV. The Seven Triunities — The Balance Wheel of Infinity
p104.s4.b0: The key to the seven triunities is that the Universal Father is always the primal member of each. He is the Absolute Center, the Primal Cause, and the Limitless Energizer.

p104.s4.b3: The contrast between the first and second triunities stands out. The first concerns evolving personalities; the second concerns evolving universes. In religious experience we meet the God who is love, but that insight must never eclipse our recognition of the cosmic fact of the pattern which is Paradise. The paper declares that the power-pattern and the loving person are one and the same universal reality.
p104.s4.b5: The description of the fourth triunity is especially vivid. The endless possibilities of the Unqualified Absolute center around the absolutum of the Isle of Paradise, and from what would otherwise be static quiescence there emanate unimaginable agitations. The paper pictures the material heart of the infinite cosmos throbbing in harmony with the Father’s plan.
p104.s4.b6: The paper discloses that there are fifteen triune associations of the First Source and Center, eight of which are not revealed; these concern realities beyond the level of supremacy. The triunities do not add to the Father’s infinity, but they make possible subinfinite and subabsolute expressions of his reality, disclosing new values and meanings.
p104.s5.h: V. Triodities — The Emergence of Experiential Deity
p104.s5.b0: There are also triune relationships of which the Father is not a member. These are not true triunities and are called triodities, among other names. The paper presents two of them.

p104.s5.b2: Where the triunities are chiefly concerned with the functional unification of infinity, the triodities are directly concerned with the appearance of the experiential Deities: Supreme, Ultimate, and Absolute. Their synthesis appears in the Supreme Being.
p104.s6.b0: Paper 104 is one of the most abstract in The Urantia Book, yet beneath it lie insights that touch daily life. Personality seeks relationship; unity coordinates diversity rather than erasing it. Love and law, personality and pattern, are not opposites but two manifestations of a single Source.

p104.s6.b2: The next paper, Paper 105, “Deity and Reality,” examines more deeply and philosophically how the seven Absolutes mentioned here were differentiated from the I AM.
p105.lead: Where does all reality come from? The paper that traces the lineage of reality from the I AM to the Seven Absolutes, and on into the finite and the transcendental.

p105.foot.text: Presented by a Melchizedek of Nebadon

p105.s0.h: Introduction — Picturing Infinity as an Ellipse
p105.s0.b0: Paper 105 is one of the most philosophical papers in The Urantia Book. Its author, a Melchizedek of Nebadon, admits his limits from the outset. Even to high orders of universe intelligences, infinity is only partially comprehensible, and the finality of reality only relatively understandable. So he suggests that we picture eternity-infinity as an almost limitless ellipse, produced by one absolute cause, moving through endless diversification, and ever seeking an infinite potential of destiny.
p105.s0.b2: The author tells us he makes the attempt knowing full well that his concepts must suffer profound distortion as they are brought down to the level of mortal understanding. We do well, then, to read this paper not as a precise blueprint but as a humble gesture toward what cannot be fathomed.
p105.s1.h: I. The Philosophic Concept of the I AM — and the Face of the Father
p105.s1.b0: The philosophers of the universes attribute absolute primal causation in infinity to the Universal Father functioning as the I AM. The I AM is the Infinite and is also infinity. He is neither deified nor undeified, neither personal nor impersonal. No qualification can be applied to him except the statement that the I AM is.
p105.s1.b1: Presenting this idea to human minds carries real dangers. It is so remote from experience that it easily distorts meanings and leads to misconceptions of values. The author therefore makes one thing clear: in all personality meanings and values, the I AM is the same as the First Person of Deity, the Universal Father of all personalities.
p105.s1.b2: Because the finite mind needs a beginning, the text imagines a hypothetical static moment in the infinitely distant past. At that moment infinity is filled by the Infinite and there is no differentiation at all; actuals are still contained within their potentials, and potentials have not yet appeared within the I AM. Yet even then, we must assume the possibility of self-will.
p105.s1.b4: This sentence anchors the whole paper. The Father we worship is that phase of the Infinite which we actually experience in our personalities, while the I AM remains our hypothesis for all that we feel is unknowable. Even the immensity of the master universe may be only a partial revelation of the Infinite, yet our concepts of infinity will keep growing throughout our endless careers.
p105.s2.h: II–III. The I AM as Triune and as Sevenfold; The Seven Absolutes of Infinity
p105.s2.b0: The seven absolute realities—the three existential persons of Deity, the Isle of Paradise, and the three Absolutes—are all co-ordinately eternal and without beginning. To explain them to human beings, however, we must arrange them in the language of time. The text postulates a “first” volitional expression and a “first” repercussional reaction within the I AM, and describes how this self-differentiation expands from a dual to a triune conception, and then to a sevenfold self-relationship.

p105.s2.b3: The first phase can be partially experienced on spiritual levels even by mortals still in the flesh, through worship. The creative acts of the third phase are always marked by unity, because they reflect outwardly the oneness of the Father-Son and of the Trinity. The seventh phase is the one that embraces everything.
p105.s2.b6: Section 3 introduces the seven Absolutes one by one. The statement that touches us most closely concerns the Second Source and Center. Without the action and aid of this absolute pattern for all personalities, no personality can reach the spirit levels of existence.
p105.s2.b8: The Isle of Paradise is the absolute of patterns and the foundation of gravity control. The eternal Isle is absolutely at rest, while all other organized energy is in motion. The Conjoint Actor integrates the cosmic energies of Paradise with the spirit energies of the Son and is the source of mind. The Deity Absolute is the destiny inceptor; the Unqualified Absolute is a quiescence that even eternity cannot exhaust; and the Universal Absolute compensates the tension between the two.
p105.s2.b10: To human minds the First Source and Center appears to come before all the other Absolutes, yet the Son, the Spirit, the three Absolutes, and the Paradise Isle coexist with him eternally. This relationship cannot be stated in the language of time without paradox. Even so, it is both fact and truth that all reality rests on the eternal existence and relationships of the seven Absolutes.
p105.s3.b0: It has sometimes been said that unity begets duality, that duality begets triunity, and that triunity is the eternal ancestor of all things. The text arranges this old intuition into three great classes of primordial relationships.

head: Relationship

Between the sevenfold I AM and the Seven Absolutes
The functional associations of the Seven Absolutes

p105.s3.b3: Pre-existentials become existential in the seven Absolutes, and existentials become functional in the triunities. Once the universe stage is thus set, cosmic energy diversifies, Paradise spirit spreads out, and mind and personality are bestowed. All of these are unified in experience on the creature level.
p105.s4.h: V–VI. Promulgation of Finite Reality and Its Repercussions
p105.s4.b0: The possibility of the finite lies within the Infinite, but it was the free will of the First Source and Center that made it actual. Only the infinity of the Father’s will could so qualify the absolute level as to create a finite. With that act begins the growth cycle—a majestic downsweep from the heights of infinity to the finite, forever swinging back inward toward Paradise—and time itself comes into being.
p105.s4.b1: The author adds that although he tells this as a sequence, transcendentals both preceded and succeeded all that is finite. Transcendental ultimates are both the cause and the consummation of the finite. The volitional act that promulgates the finite also means a qualification of absoluteness and the appearance of relativities.

p105.s4.b3: What grows in time must look incomplete, but this difference, so important on this side of Paradise, does not exist in eternity. The promulgation of the finite set off repercussions in Deity, in the universe, and among creatures.

p105.s4.b6: To attain perfection through evolution implies a starting point that is not perfect, and so misadaptation and conflict are inherent in evolutionary growth. Yet this very time lag makes creatures participants in divine creation. It is worth noticing that the text explains both the possibility of evil and our partnership with God from the same root.
p105.s5.h: VII. Eventuation of Transcendentals — Between the Finite and the Absolute
p105.s5.b0: Transcendentals are subinfinite and subabsolute, yet superfinite and supercreatural—an integrating level. To creatures they appear to follow from the finite; from the eternity viewpoint they anticipate it. Havona illustrates the paradox. It is neither absolute nor an evolutionary creation, and it acts as a buffer between Paradise and the finite creations.

p105.s5.b3: As the Supreme is associated with finites, so the Ultimate is identified with transcendentals—but the difference between them is one of quality, not merely of degree. Our universe exists on finite, transcendental, and absolute levels, and it is unified absolutely by the triunities, functionally by the Architects of the Master Universe, and relatively by the Seven Master Spirits.
p105.s5.b4: God the Sevenfold reveals the personality and divinity of the Universal Father to creatures of both maximum and submaximum status. The forces of the Absolutes, the spirits of the Deities, and the personalities of the Gods, which stirred in the eternal past in response to the primordial self-will, now echo in this universe age as the vast cosmic panorama before our eyes.
p105.s6.b0: Paper 105 deals with heights that can make the head spin, but its conclusion is simple. The face the Infinite turns toward us is the face of a loving Father, and in him we all live and move. Even the imperfection of evolution is a space left open so that we might become partners in divine creation. The text also leaves open the possibility that the diversification of original reality may go on, onward and outward, age after age.

p105.s6.b2: The next paper, Paper 106, “Universe Levels of Reality,” continues by examining how the levels unfolded here—finite, transcendental, and absolute—are progressively integrated through the Supreme Being and the Ultimate.
